title: C168 — 6R80 transmission assembly connector
introduction:
This transmission connector brings shaft-speed, range and fluid-temperature signals together with solenoid controls, supply and return circuits. I treat its face drawing as an address map: the scattered cavity labels locate electrical connections, not the order in which the gearbox changes gear.

Begin with the connector identification table, find a cavity label in the circular drawing, then read its complete assignment row. That joins a physical position on the illustration to a circuit identity and function. This is a reference-reading guide; connector access, release, probing, wire selection and replacement need separate instructions. The physical viewing side, Size codes and gauge convention are not defined here.

edits.why: On the page, the long external projection extends toward the lower left, while a bridge-like feature crosses part of the face on the right. I use those shapes and the internal cutouts to keep my place because the cavity labels do not form a simple grid. The shaded position corresponds to the assignment row with no circuit details and an unused indication. Shading helps connect the drawing to that row; it is not a diagnosis of the connector's condition. The illustration does not establish a release movement or physical viewing side.

Match the drawing's cavity label to Cavity, then read across for Circuit Number, Color, Gauge, Function, Qualifier, Used and Terminal Part Number. The function descriptions separate sensor information, pressure and shift solenoid controls, solenoid power control, buffered sensor supply and signal returns. Keep the abbreviations and bracketed labels attached to their descriptions when using another wiring reference. A signal-return label does not make that row interchangeable with every other return circuit. The blank assignment is retained as documented; it does not call for adding a wire. These entries identify connections without supplying expected readings or proving that a sensor or solenoid works.

The pigtail entry describes a connector with attached wire leads and keeps its kit identification, listed gauge, material, cavity count, image filename, service part and engineering shell together. I compare Engineering Shell with Hard Shell to follow the documented connector association. Use the terminal part entry belonging to the individual circuit row when reading terminal identification; the pigtail listing is a separate service entry. Neither its gauge nor its cavity count supplies a splicing method or a replacement-wire specification.
